newsitem.title: LEBANON: Syria-backed candidates poised to win Lebanon vote.
newsitem.headline: Syria-backed candidates poised to win Lebanon vote.

text.p: Syrian-backed candidates headed to a crushing victory in the last round of Lebanon's general election, sweeping all but one of the 23 Bekaa Valley parliamentary seats, partial results on Monday showed.

Voter turnout in the eastern Bekka Valley, 52 percent of the 408,770 eligible voters according to the interior ministry, was higher than in any other region, where pro-Syrian candidates had won an overwhelming majority in four earlier rounds.

Partial results of Sunday's vote in the Bekka that determines the final shape of the 128-seat house showed a Syrian-brokered list including six ministers, several deputies and candidates of Hizbollah and the secular Amal, Lebanon's two main Shi'ite Moslem movements, winning 22 seats.
A 10-man leftist ticket headed by Communist Party leader Farouk Dharouje and a six-man list of independents both lost.

If official results expected later on Monday confirm this, Hizbollah, which is fighting Israeli troops in south Lebanon, would have scored a political comeback in the last two rounds in the Bekaa and south Lebanon after defeats in earlier rounds.
The fundamentalist group would end up with seven deputies and two supporters compared with eight MPs and four supporters in the outgoing assembly.

Two Hizbollah MPs lost their seats in earlier rounds of voting but four candidates won in south Lebanon polls last Sunday under an election deal with Amal brokered by Syria, Lebanon's main foreign power broker. The Amal-Hizbollah alliance continued in the Bekaa vote.

Political sources said Syria greatly influenced the makeup of the list -- a disparate group of rivals all viewed however as allies of Syria -- to prevent the election of politicians it dislikes and to avert a showdown at the ballot box between Amal and Hizbollah in the mainly Shi'ite regions.
Turnout was initially reported to be low but Interior Minister Michel al-Murr told reporters on Sunday night that it shot up to about 52 percent of the Bekaa's eligible voters before polls closed.

Beirut newspapers said voting was extended by as much as two hours at some polling stations due to a last-minute surge as rival candidates urged many supporters to vote then after reports of widespread crossing off of names from ballot papers.

Polls observers said Christians in particular were crossing Hizbollah and its supporters off their ballot papers as they were angered that a Maronite Christian on the list was chosen by Hizbollah under the deal brokered by Syria.
The Lebanese Association for the Democracy of Elections (LADE), an independent watchdog, reported many irregularities in the poll. It reported widespread abuses in the earlier rounds.

LADE cited illegal presence of security forces in hundreds of polling stations, candidate monitors prohibited from entering polling stations, one incident of illegal voting in the name of a dead person and extensive mistakes in voter lists.

"The mistakes in the voter lists were far more extensive than the mistakes that had existed in the voter lists in 1992; such an increase could only take place intentionally. This raised complaints and accusations the government was continuing to use voter lists as a way to manipulate the outcome of the elections," LADE said in a statement.
